passage:
Subject: Day two, and the end of my plan
Hi Seema,
You asked how the new routine is going, so: it isn't. On the first of January I woke at five, ran three laps of the campus ground, did two hours of revision and ticked every box on a chart. On day two my alarm rang and I slept through it. I looked at the empty box and thought, that's it, the streak is dead. By evening I had peeled the chart off the wall, skipped the run, the revision and dinner in the mess, and eaten biscuits in bed. It has been ten days. One bad morning should not have wiped out everything, but at the time it felt like all or nothing. Maybe I'll try again on Monday with a smaller plan. Tell me I'm not hopeless. 🙂
Wasim

qa.q: What did Wasim do on the first of January before revising?
qa.a: Wasim woke at five and ran three laps of the campus ground.

qa.q: What was Wasim thinking when looking at the empty box on the chart?
qa.a: That the streak was dead and the whole plan was ruined, a discouraged all-or-nothing thought.

qa.q: What could Wasim change in the plan for Monday?
qa.a: Make it smaller and allow one missed morning without dropping everything else, so a slip stays a slip.

qa.q: How might Seema read the line asking to be told Wasim is not hopeless?
qa.a: As a request for reassurance. Seema would likely see someone discouraged rather than lazy and may reply kindly. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who starts an ambitious routine and abandons it after one missed morning.

passage: So, Parveen, here is my confession for this year, from Anand the timetable person. On the first of January I made a timetable for my final-year project: five hours of coding every day, no phone, in bed by ten, colour-coded. I did it perfectly for nine days. On day ten my cousin's wedding ran late and I got home at two. I skipped the morning session, and by afternoon I was telling myself, well, the streak's gone, might as well start fresh in February. February became March. The funny part is that all I had really missed was one day. If I had just opened the laptop for twenty minutes that evening, the whole thing would have kept going. Now I do a plain thirty minutes and the code is actually moving.

qa.q: How long did Anand keep the timetable going perfectly?
qa.a: Anand did it perfectly for nine days.

qa.q: What was Anand thinking when the late wedding made the morning session impossible?
qa.a: That one missed session had ruined everything, an all-or-nothing thought mixed with disappointment.

qa.q: What could Anand have done on the evening of day ten?
qa.a: Anand could have opened the laptop for even twenty minutes so the routine kept going.

qa.q: How might Parveen react to hearing this confession?
qa.a: Parveen might recognise a few January plans of the same kind and would probably see Anand as honest rather than lazy. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a young adult whose ambitious study routine ended after the first missed day because of all-or-nothing thinking.

passage:
Hostel sports coach's note, second week of January.
On 1 January, Yogesh came to me with a printed plan: a 5 a.m. run every day, weights every evening, no sugar, and cold showers. He was glowing. I suggested starting with three days a week. He said, "No half measures this year."
He kept it for eight days. I saw him on the track each morning, grimly pushing.
On the ninth day it rained heavily and he stayed in bed. When I saw him that afternoon, he said, "It's ruined now. I broke the streak." He looked embarrassed and angry at himself.
He has not come to the track since. When I asked, he said, "Maybe I'm just not a fitness person."
I will sit with him this week and suggest a smaller plan: three short runs, and a rule that a missed day is just a missed day, not the end of the plan.
— Vandana, sports coach

qa.q: How many days did Yogesh keep the plan?
qa.a: He kept it for eight days.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel after the rainy morning?
qa.a: Yogesh felt embarrassed and angry at himself, believing one missed day had ruined everything.

qa.q: What small change is the coach planning, and why might it help?
qa.a: Three short runs a week and a rule that a missed day is not the end, so one lapse doesn't turn into quitting.

qa.q: How might Vandana have felt when Yogesh said "No half measures"?
qa.a: Vandana was probably doubtful and a bit worried, having seen big plans collapse before.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who starts an ambitious routine and quits after the first missed day, as all-or-nothing thinking takes over.

passage:
7 January.
New year plan, day 7. Or it was.
The plan: wake at 5, study three hours before college, no phone until lunch, gym every evening. I made a colour-coded sheet and stuck it above my bed. Days one to five, perfect. I felt like a completely new person.
Yesterday was Yogesh's birthday. We were out till midnight. This morning my alarm went at 5, and I switched it off and slept till 8:30. When I woke up and saw the time, I felt sick. Six days of perfect, ruined.
I didn't study at all today. I didn't go to the gym. I scrolled my phone for two hours. If the streak is broken, what's the point?
Writing this down, it sounds ridiculous. One late morning, and I threw away the whole day too.
Tomorrow: 6 a.m., one hour of study. Not three. Let's see if Disha can do a smaller version.

qa.q: Why did the narrator sleep late this morning?
qa.a: Yesterday was Yogesh's birthday, and they were out till midnight.

qa.q: How did Disha feel on waking at 8:30?
qa.a: Disha felt sick and defeated, believing the six perfect days were ruined.

qa.q: What does Disha decide for tomorrow, and why is it wiser?
qa.a: Disha plans 6 a.m. and one hour instead of three, a smaller version that is easier to keep after a lapse.

qa.q: How might Yogesh feel on hearing about the ruined streak?
qa.a: Yogesh might feel a little guilty about the late night, and surprised that one morning led Disha to drop the whole day.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose ambitious new-year routine collapses after one missed morning because of all-or-nothing thinking.

passage:
Bidisha: ok I'm quitting the 30-day yoga thing
Neelam: what?? you were on day 6!
Bidisha: I missed today. cousin's wedding, no time
Bidisha: so the challenge is broken. 30 days means 30 days
Neelam: so do day 7 tomorrow
Bidisha: it doesn't count if there's a gap
Neelam: says who? the app?
Bidisha: says me I guess 😞
Neelam: Bidisha. you did 6 days. that's 6 more than last year
Bidisha: feels like failing
Neelam: missing one day at a wedding isn't failing. quitting because of it is the only way you actually lose
Bidisha: hmm
Neelam: tomorrow do 10 minutes. just 10. I'll do it with you on video
Bidisha: ok fine. 10 minutes
Neelam: 🙂

qa.q: Why did Bidisha miss the yoga today?
qa.a: Cousin's wedding, no time.

qa.q: How does Bidisha feel about missing day 7?
qa.a: Bidisha feels discouraged, as if the whole challenge has failed because of one missed day.

qa.q: What does Neelam suggest, and why does it help?
qa.a: Doing just ten minutes tomorrow together on video, which makes restarting small and easy after the lapse.

qa.q: How does Neelam see the six days Bidisha already did?
qa.a: Neelam sees them as real progress, six more days than last year, not wasted effort.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who wants to quit a routine after one missed day, and a friend who challenges the all-or-nothing thinking.

passage:
On the first of January, Rashmi taped a chart to the wall of her room in Palampur: run to the tea gardens at five, fifty push-ups, one hour of English, no sweets. She drew thirty boxes for the month.
For five days she ticked every box, breath steaming in the cold, and showed her sister Jyoti the chart each night.
On the sixth day, her cousin's wedding ran till two in the morning. She slept through the alarm, ate three laddoos at breakfast, and stared at the empty box.
"That's it. It's ruined," she said.
"It's one day," said Jyoti.
"The chart's spoiled now." Rashmi took it down and folded it into a drawer. She didn't run on the seventh day, or the eighth. By the end of January the English book had a layer of dust on it, and the chart was still in the drawer, with five ticks.

qa.q: For how many days did Rashmi tick every box?
qa.a: For five days she ticked every box.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she said "It's ruined"?
qa.a: Rashmi felt disappointed and defeated, seeing one missed day as spoiling the whole chart.

qa.q: What could Rashmi try after a missed day like the wedding?
qa.a: Rashmi could just pick up the next day, even with a shorter run or half an hour of English, instead of treating one gap as the end.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see the missed day?
qa.a: Jyoti sees it as just one day, not a reason to stop, which is why Jyoti says, "It's one day."

grounding: Shows a young adult starting an ambitious routine with energy and abandoning all of it after the first missed day.
